name: Oil lamp, simple
note: Simple clay and bronze oil lamps, burning olive oil or animal fat, are already everywhere there is oil or fat to spare. The innovation ahead is the flat wick and glass chimney, which doubles brightness.

name: Tallow candle
note: Cheap animal-fat candles; smoky and foul-smelling but accessible to the poor. Tallow is rendered from beef and mutton fat.

name: Soft soap from tallow and ash lye
note: Rendered fat boiled with a lye leached from wood ash gives a soft soap, a craft practice in northern Europe long before the chemistry of saponification was understood. The later saponification technique explains it and improves yield and hardness; it is not needed to make the soap.

name: Beeswax candle
note: Expensive, clean-burning, fragrant. Beeswax is a byproduct of honey extraction and remains expensive through the early modern period.

name: Flush latrine with running water
note: Flush latrines connected to running water and sewers are already established wherever that infrastructure exists (Rome is the best-documented case), but lack the water trap. Sewer gas backs up into the house at night when flow stops. This is the fatal gap.

name: Lead and ceramic plumbing
note: Lead pipe-making and ceramic drainage are already mastered wherever there is a developed urban water system (Rome is the best-documented case). The lead slowly poisons users, who generally attribute the symptoms to other causes.

name: Hypocaust underfloor heating
note: Hot air from a furnace flows through hollow spaces beneath the floor. Expensive; only wealthy houses and public baths use it. Without the chimney, which most of the ancient world lacks, room heating otherwise requires a brazier and open flame.

name: Public bath (thermae)
note: Public hygiene infrastructure at this scale is remarkable for its era wherever it exists (Rome's thermae are the model: heated water pools, caldarium and frigidarium as social centres); even so, most private homes still lack hot water.

copy_visibility_reason: A mirror shows its shape but not the tin-rich alloy and the polish that make it bright, and the Chinese magic mirrors puzzled European makers who studied them.
name: Mirror, polished bronze
note: Polished bronze reflects poorly (70-80% at best) and tarnishes. Small, expensive, and slowly replaced by silvered glass mirrors.

name: Glass windows, wealthy houses
note: Rare and expensive. Glassblowing technology exists, but glass remains thick, poorly transparent, and valuable. Most windows are oil-paper or shutters.

name: Wooden furniture
note: Chairs, tables, beds, and chests. Quality varies from crude to fine (imported citrus wood). Beds are typically frames with rope supports, no springs.

name: Board games, dice games, and pieces
note: Latrunculi (small stones on a board), duodecim scripta (twelve marks, ancestor of backgammon), and knucklebones for gaming. Dice are carved bone or stone.

name: Musical instruments
note: Lyres, kitharas, flutes, Pan pipes, and percussion. All handmade; quality varies by maker. String instruments require catgut or sinew from animals.

name: Perfume by enfleurage
note: Flower petals are laid on cold fat, which absorbs fragrance. Repeated; expensive and used by the wealthy. Yields poor revenue; the innovation is distillation for concentrates.

name: Roman cosmetics
note: Powders, kohl eyeliner, rouge, and white lead face paint (cerussa). The white lead is cosmetically effective but chronically poisoning users. No warning label exists.

name: Locks and keys
note: Pin-tumbler locks exist already in Egypt, and excellent examples in bronze and iron exist wherever there is skilled metalworking (Rome's are especially well attested). Locks are expensive and a sign of wealth (or slavery).

copy_visibility_reason: A bar of soap does not show the lye, the fat or the salting out, though a soap-boiler's yard can be seen in operation.
name: Hard soap, sapo
note: Hot saponification of animal fat and plant oil with caustic lye, producing hard soap. Rome lacks this; soap is invented in the Eastern Mediterranean around 6th century. Labour-intensive but small-scale.

name: Fireplace and chimney
note: The chimney is missing from most of the ancient world's architecture at this point (Rome never develops it). The innovation is the flue and draft that draws smoke out of a room while allowing air intake from below. Transforms cold-weather living. Early chimneys are smoky and dangerous; the design improves over centuries.

name: Enclosed stove
note: A metal or ceramic box with fire inside, heating room air by radiation and conduction. More efficient than open fireplace because less heat escapes up the chimney. Requires cast iron or tile manufacture.

name: Latrine water trap (S-bend)
note: The water trap is the critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the toilet bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Non-obvious but essential for sanitary plumbing. Rome discovers this late or not at all in the West.

name: Spectacles, corrective lenses
note: Convex lenses for presbyopia (age-related farsightedness) arrive around 1300. Concave lenses for myopia come later. The hinge and bridge are crafted from brass. Spectacles are luxury goods until mass production.

name: Button with eyelet
note: Buttons already exist in most of these societies, but are rare and made of stone or bone. The eyelet (sewn loop) adds cost. Horn buttons become viable later with better tools. Buttons displace expensive brooches, freeing wealth.

name: Pencil, graphite in wood
note: Graphite pencils arrive in the 16th century after graphite discovery in Cumberland. Early designs slot graphite into wood holders; later hexagonal wood casing is carved around it. Graphite is cheap once located; supply is the constraint.

name: Toothbrush
note: Bone or wood handle with bristles of horsehair or bamboo fiber. Romans use twigs and charcoal powder for dental cleaning. The toothbrush format is luxury; mass adoption requires cheap bristles and handles.

name: Friction matches
note: White phosphorus matches ignite easily but cause phosphorus necrosis (rotting jawbone) in workers from chronic exposure. Safety matches use red phosphorus instead, less toxic. Early matches are dangerous to makers and users alike.

name: Umbrella
note: Wood frame with linen canopy. Rome and later cultures have parasols (sun protection); rain umbrellas arrive in northern Europe around 1500s. Widespread adoption requires industrial metal frames and waterproof cotton textiles.

name: Mirror, silvered glass
note: Mercury and tin amalgam fused to glass back creates a reflective layer (90%+ vs 70% for bronze). Expensive and technically demanding; production moves to Venice in the 13th century. Frames are precious metal or fine wood.

name: Safety pin
note: Bent iron wire with a catch. Simpler than brooches and more secure for fastening cloth or diapers. Mass production requires drawn wire and stamping, both later innovations.

name: Eraser, breadcrumb substitute
note: Breadcrumbs (white bread preferred) erase pencil marks by mechanical abrasion. Later rubber erasers require natural rubber, which is UNOBTAINABLE. Breadcrumb remains the substitute through the 19th century in resource-limited settings.

name: Playing cards, printed
note: Woodcut or engraved cards printed in volume. Early printed decks (15th century) are hand-coloured. Standardised designs (Italian, Spanish, French suits) emerge later. Cards were originally hand-painted and very expensive.

name: Jigsaw puzzle
note: Hand-cut wooden jigsaw (using a saw, hence the name). Early puzzles are mounted hand-coloured prints glued to wood, then sawn into interlocking pieces. Expensive and educational for wealthy families.

name: Argand oil lamp
note: The flat circular wick and glass chimney allow air circulation from both sides of the flame, increasing brightness 3x over simple lamps. The chimney creates draft, keeping the flame in the hot zone. Oil consumption stays the same; light output soars.

name: Pocket watch
note: Miniaturized spring-driven mechanism with balance wheel (spiral spring regulating oscillation). Requires high precision machining and jeweled pivots to reduce friction. Early watches lose 5-10 minutes per day; later escapements improve accuracy.

name: Mechanical clock for home
note: Escapement mechanism converts continuous power (falling weight or spring) into regulated ticks. Medieval clocks are weight-driven with iron verge escapement; later designs use springs. Accuracy improves from hours to minutes as escapements advance.

name: Kitchen range (cast iron)
note: A fireplace-integrated cooking structure with a hot surface (cooking plate) and an oven. Cast iron conducts heat evenly. Requires blast furnace for casting; transforms cooking from dangling pots over flames. Labour-displacing for kitchen servants (negative gov).

name: Pressure cooker (Papin's digester)
note: A sealed vessel where steam pressure raises water boiling point, accelerating cooking 3x. Papin invents the digester in 1679 to demonstrate steam power; it becomes both a cooking device AND the conceptual ancestor of the steam engine. Requires safety valve.

name: Metronome
note: Pendulum-driven clock ticking at adjustable rates for musical practice. Inverted design pivots the weight on a rod. Musicians find it essential; composers use metronome markings to standardise tempo. Early metronomes are wooden; later all-metal designs are more durable.

name: Kerosene lamp
note: Kerosene (paraffin) burns hotter and cleaner than whale oil or plant oil. Brighter than Argand lamps with less smoke. Requires refined petroleum; supply depends on oil fields and distillation capacity.

name: Piano with hammer action
note: Struck strings with escapement mechanism allowing rapid re-strike. Cristofori invents the hammer action around 1700, replacing plucked harpsichords. Touche and dynamic range enable entirely new music. Expensive; requires years of training to play well.

name: Sprung mattress
note: Coiled iron springs in a wood frame topped with ticking and stuffing (wool, horsehair, or coconut fiber). Dramatically more comfortable than rope-frame beds. Requires drawn wire and coil-forming tools. Mass production follows industrial tooling.

name: Sewing machine, hand-crank
note: Reciprocating needle driven by crank mechanism. Howe and Singer commercialize sewing machines in the 1850s; hand-crank models precede treadle and electric drives. Stitches much faster than hand-sewing; domestic servants' value plummets.

name: Perfume, distilled alcohol base
note: Alcohol dissolves and carries fragrance far better than fat alone. Volatile alcohols evaporate, leaving scent on skin and clothes. Concentrated distilled perfumes (attar) command high prices and excellent margins. The innovation is distillation, not enfleurage.

name: Printed books for home
note: Printed volumes replace hand-copied manuscripts. Early books are expensive; gradually price falls as standardisation and competition reduce costs. Literacy spreads; libraries become personal, not institutional.

name: Washing machine, hand-powered
note: A wooden or metal tub with paddles or rollers rotated by crank. Hot soapy water and mechanical action replace hours of hand-scrubbing. Laundry maids become surplus; wealthy households buy machines rather than slaves.

name: Mangle and wringer
note: Paired hard rollers (wood or stone) squeeze water from cloth under pressure. Early mangling flattens linen; later wringer versions extract water faster. Eliminates the wringing-by-hand step; hand-wringer maids face unemployment.

name: Toys and dolls
note: Carved wooden dolls with jointed limbs or cloth bodies. Lead and tin soldiers for boys; fashion dolls for girls. Decoration and articulation increase cost. Toys become a significant retail category in the 18th and 19th centuries.

name: Gas lamp and gasolier
note: Coal-gas (coke-oven gas) piped to rooms. Brighter than oil lamps but smoky and dangerous (carbon monoxide, explosions). Gas lighting spreads in cities; rural areas remain oil-lit for decades. Gasolier chandeliers replace candles in urban mansions.

name: Safety razor
note: Replaceable blade held at a fixed angle in a handle guard, preventing deep cuts. Earlier straight razors require stropping and honing; safety razors are simpler for users. Gillette disposable blades (early 1900s) create a consumable product with huge margins.

name: Zip fastener
note: Interlocking teeth or loops fastened by sliding slider. Whitcomb L. Judson invents the 'clasp locker' in 1891; Gideon Sundback perfects the modern zip in 1913. Requires precision stamping and assembly. Replaces buttons for boots and jackets.

name: Fountain pen
note: Ink reservoir under the nib, with capillary feed. Early designs leak; improved feeds (Waterman, Parker) in the 1880s fix this. Replaces dip pens and quills. Refillable or cartridge designs follow; mass production drives prices down.

name: Carpet sweeper
note: Wheeled frame with rotating brush underneath. Push it across carpet to collect dust and lint. No electricity needed. Precedes vacuum cleaners; faster than hand-brushing. Carpet sweepers are labour-replacing and displace sweeping servants.

name: Attar of roses
note: Distilled rose oil (4 kg of petals for 1 g of oil). Extremely expensive and high-margin. Attar is one of the best early revenue products: small weight, non-perishable, high demand from the wealthy. Bulgarian and Persian atar dominate the market.

name: Shampoo, soap-based
note: Soap solution with perfume. Romans wash hair with lye (harsh) or oil. Soap-based shampoo is gentle and effective. Liquid and powdered forms compete; bars arrive later. Fragrance matters for premium products.

name: Deodorant
note: Alum or zinc oxide in a fat or powder base. Alum acts as an astringent, reducing sweat and odour; it is already used on textiles in several ancient economies (Rome's is the best-attested), and the same substance applies as readily to skin. Modern antiperspirants require aluminium chloride (20th century).

name: Double glazing (two panes)
note: Two panes of glass with an air gap reduces heat loss by half. Expensive to produce and install; assembly requires careful spacing and lead frame. Widespread only in the 18th-19th centuries as glass prices fall.

name: Refrigeration, mechanical ice machine
note: Ammonia or ether evaporation in a compressor cools an ice chamber. Requires a steam engine to drive the compressor. Early mechanical ice-makers (Carve, 1850s) free wealthy households from dependence on natural ice harvesting and storage.

name: Electric lighting in home
note: Incandescent bulbs (Edison carbon, then tungsten filament) or arc lamps. Grid electricity required. Replaces gas lamps and kerosene. Cost per lumen falls; brightness increases. Urban electrification spreads from 1880s onward.

name: Electric fan for air circulation
note: Small electric motor drives a blade assembly. Expensive initially; prices fall with mass production. A hot climate values this enormously, wherever you find one; ceiling punkah fans pulled by servants are the low-tech precursor.

name: Ceiling punkah, servant-pulled
note: A large cloth fan suspended from the ceiling, pulled by a cord to and fro by a servant. Provides air circulation and cooling in hot climates. Entirely mechanical and labour-intensive; electric fans are the obvious 19th-century replacement.

name: Vacuum cleaner
note: Electric motor drives a suction fan that pulls dirt through a cloth bag filter. Replaces carpet sweepers and hand-brushing entirely. Servants become redundant. Cord length and motor noise are early limitations; wireless and quiet models come later.

name: Dishwasher, mechanical and electric
note: Cochran's 1886 machine uses pressurised water spray, hot water, and soap. Requires a pressurised water supply (pump), a heat source (steam or electric), and a motor. Hot water and soap do most of the work; the machine's innovation is automation and pressure. Kitchen staff is displaced.

name: Flush toilet with S-bend water trap
note: The water trap is the non-obvious critical innovation: standing water in an S-bend or U-bend below the bowl blocks sewer gas from backing into the house. Crapper patents an improved design in 1884. Modern plumbing code mandates traps.

name: Sewer separated from stormwater drain
note: Sewage and rain runoff follow separate pipes to prevent sewage backup during storms. Public health innovation; requires city-scale investment. Many 19th-century cities combine sewers (causing problems); separation is a later upgrade.

name: Bath with piped hot water
note: A boiler (steam-driven or later electric) supplies hot water on demand. Luxurious; middle-class homes gain hot water later than wealthy houses. Requires pressurised pipes and heating infrastructure. Modern thermostatic mixing valves prevent scalding.

name: Central heating by hot water radiator
note: Boiler in basement or furnace room heats water, which circulates through cast-iron radiators in all rooms. Replaces fireplaces and central stove heating. Enables uniform comfort; transforms house design. Requires piping, a circulating pump, and constant fuel supply.

name: Washing machine, electric-powered
note: Motor-driven drum or agitator. No cranking required. Faster cycles, cooler operation, less wear on fabric. Laundry becomes a household task rather than a full-time servant job. Early motors are noisy and prone to breakage; reliability improves.

name: Home refrigerator, electric
note: Domestic refrigerator with electric compressor. Freon (CFC) replaces ammonia for safety (1930s). Standard feature in wealthy homes by 1950s; middle-class penetration spreads with electrification and price falls. Transforms food preservation and cooking.

name: Clothes dryer, electric tumble
note: A perforated drum tumbles wet laundry through warm air, driven by an electric motor and heated by a resistance element, replacing the clothesline and the mangle. A distinct invention from the washing machine itself, not a variant of it: Sampson patents a hand-cranked ventilating drum dryer in 1892, but the first practical automatic electric one is Hamilton Manufacturing's 1938 'Thor Automagic', which puts the drum, the motor and a thermostatically controlled heater in one cabinet. It needs nothing the electric washer has not already put in the house except the heating element.

name: Domestic deep freezer
note: Not a colder refrigerator: holding about -18C rather than +4C needs a larger-duty compressor, several times the insulation thickness, and a refrigerant charge and evaporator sized for the lower temperature, none of which the icebox-descended refrigerator cabinet provides. What actually pulls it into American homes through the 1940s is not the compressor, already solved by hom_refrigerator_home_electric, but the frozen-food industry giving people something worth freezing: Clarence Birdseye's flash-freezing process, commercialised from 1930, makes frozen food palatable enough to want months of storage rather than an icebox's days.

name: Cosmetics with safety warnings
note: Once germ theory and toxicology establish that white lead causes chronic poisoning, cosmetics reformulate. Lead face paint is phased out; zinc oxide and iron oxides replace it. Labels warn of hazards. Modern cosmetics prioritise safety and truthful marketing.

name: Toothpaste, commercial formulation
note: Soap base with abrasive chalk or pumice powder, flavoured. Early toothpastes are gritty; fluoride is added in the 1950s. Toothbrushes + paste replace charcoal and salt rubbing. Marketing drives adoption; modern formulations include whiteners and stain removers.

name: Fashion doll with clothing sets
note: Articulated wooden or bisque doll with interchangeable clothing. Allows girls to dress dolls in fashionable gowns. Drives textile consumption and toy industry growth. Later porcelain and plastic dolls command higher prices; bisque allows fine detail.

name: Vacuum flask, thermos
note: Double-walled glass with vacuum between walls and silvered inner surface. Dewar invents it in 1892 for laboratory use; commercial thermos bottles follow. Keeps hot drinks hot for hours; cold drinks cold. Expensive; mass production eventually lowers cost.
